title: Chinese mythology
description: Mythology of the greater Chinese area
wiki_lead:
Chinese mythology (traditional Chinese: 中國神話; simplified Chinese: 中国神话; pinyin: Zhōngguó shénhuà), is mythology that has been passed down in oral form or recorded in literature throughout the area now known as Greater China. Chinese mythology encompasses a diverse array of myths derived from regional and cultural traditions. Populated with engaging narratives featuring extraordinary individuals and beings endowed with magical powers, these stories often unfold in fantastical mythological realms or historical epochs. Similar to numerous other mythologies, Chinese mythology has historically been regarded, at least partially, as a factual record of the past.
Along with Chinese folklore, Chinese mythology forms an important part of Chinese folk religion and of religious Taoism. Many narratives recounting characters and events from ancient times exhibit a dual tradition: one that presents a more historicized or euhemerized interpretation, and another that offers a more mythological perspective.
Numerous myths delve into the creation and cosmology of the universe, exploring the origins of deities and heavenly inhabitants. Some narratives specifically address the topic of creation, unraveling the beginnings of things, people, and culture. Additionally, certain myths are dedicated to the genesis of the Chinese state. A subset of myths provides a chronology of prehistoric times, often featuring a culture hero who taught people essential skills ranging from building houses and cooking to the basics of writing. In some cases, they were revered as the ancestor of an ethnic group or dynastic families. Chinese mythology is intimately connected to the traditional Chinese concepts of li and qi. These two foundational concepts are deeply entwined with socially oriented ritual acts, including communication, greetings, dances, ceremonies, and sacrifices.

Classification
Ancient myths: Pangu creating the world with his body, Nuwa mending the sky and creating human beings, Jingwei filling the sea, Kuafu chasing the sun, Dayu controlling the flood, Gonggong hitting Mount Buzhou in anger, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, Shennong tasting hundreds of herbs, Cangjie creating characters, Xingtian dancing with Ganqi, Suiren drilling wood to make fire, Yugong moving the mountains, and many other famous myths.
Folk myths and legends: The Legend of the White Snake, The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, Chang'e Flying to the Moon, Houyi Shooting the Sun, Wu Gang Cutting the Cassia Tree, Meng Jiangnu, Weeping Down the Great Wall, Drilling Two Woods to Make Fire, Black Dog Eating the Moon, The Butterfly Lovers, Foolish Old Man Moving Mountains, Goddess of Luo River and Mi Fei, King Mu's Journey to the West, Magu Offering Longevity, Danzhu Turning into a Bird, The Slaying of the Unicorn, Lark Exterminating the Dragon, King Wang's Crying Cuckoo, The Acacia Tree, Jigong, The Legend of New Year's Eve, The Twelve Chinese Zodiac Signs, The Carp Leaping over the Dragon Gate, The Money Tree and the Treasure Bowl, The Seven Brothers of the Yang Family, The Five Brothers, The Book from Heaven, The Legend of the Dragon Boat Festival, The Legend of Sun Moon Lake and other famous myths and legends.
Literary myths and legends: Nezha Conquers the Dragon King, Havoc in Heaven, Journey to the West, Investiture of the Gods, Splitting the Mountain to Save the Mother, The Precious Lotus Lantern and other famous myths and legends.


Mythology and religion

Significant interplay exists between Chinese mythology and the philosophical traditions of Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism. Elements of pre-Han dynasty mythology such as those in Classic of Mountains and Seas were adapted into these belief systems as they developed (in the case of Taoism), or were assimilated into Chinese culture (in the case of Buddhism). grok_lead: Chinese mythology comprises the body of myths, legends, and folk narratives historically recorded in classical Chinese texts and transmitted through oral traditions within the regions of ancient and modern China, encompassing cosmogonic accounts, divine interventions, heroic exploits, and explanations of natural phenomena and social hierarchies. Unlike unified mythological systems in other civilizations, it lacks a centralized canon or pantheon, instead presenting fragmented, regionally diverse stories often embedded in philosophical, historical, and ritualistic writings from the Warring States period (475â221 BCE) onward, with primary sources including the Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas) and Huainanzi. Central to Chinese mythology are cosmological motifs such as the primordial chaos giving way to separated heaven and earth, exemplified in late-recorded tales of Pangu's dismemberment forming the world or NÃ¼wa mending the fractured sky with colored stones, reflecting animistic and shamanistic origins tied to early agricultural and ancestral cults. Deities and semidivine heroes, including the culture-bringers Fuxi and NÃ¼wa âwho invented writing, fishing, and marriage âand the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), victor over chaotic forces like Chi You, embody ideals of order, innovation, and martial prowess, frequently euhemerized in historical chronicles to legitimize imperial rule via the Mandate of Heaven. Mythical creatures such as dragons symbolizing imperial authority and auspicious rain, phoenixes denoting harmony, and hybrid beasts in the Shanhaijing illustrate a worldview integrating yin-yang dualism and five-phase elemental cycles to interpret causality in nature and human affairs. These traditions evolved syncretically, absorbing influences from indigenous animism, Zhou dynasty ritualism, and later Buddhist and Daoist elements, while facing suppression or rationalization under Confucian orthodoxy and 20th-century ideological campaigns that prioritized materialist interpretations over supernatural narratives. Despite such discontinuities, Chinese mythology persists in festivals, temple worship, and literature, underscoring causal links between divine precedents and enduring cultural practices like filial piety and geomantic harmony.
